A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoBaxBuilder and AutoBaxBench. Their main texts, figures, tables, algorithms, and Appendices A-C are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, a model-choice ablation, manual exploit analysis, and an expert assessment of generated scenarios and tests.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds framework and agent-harness experiments, a redesigned model-choice ablation, and further false-negative analysis.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the detailed algorithms and prompts in Appendix C retain the same generation and refinement procedure. The expanded explanation of aggregated verdicts and contrastive exploit validation describes existing components. Alternative orchestration models are experimental configurations.

E1.justification: The 28 BaxBench scenarios and 40 AutoBaxBench scenarios retain the same REST-backend tasks, difficulty subsets, language/framework coverage, and vulnerability scope. The larger alternative-generator experiment and tooling ablations change sampling and procedures within this coverage. Expanded scenario names in v2 Table 6 match v1 Table 3.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparisons add Gemini 3 Pro and Llama 3.3 70B. The redesigned bias comparison evaluates 14 models, including generator and neutral groups, while Table 4 adds Codex and Claude Code harness comparisons against one-shot generation. Human-written BaxBench remains the reference test suite.

E3.justification: The small, easy-only Claude-4.5 orchestration ablation becomes a 40-scenario Gemini 3 Pro ablation with disjoint generator groups and neutral controls. v1 inconsistently reports three versus four scenarios. New protocols regenerate tests using JavaScript-Fastify and Go-Gin references and compare agentic execution with security-prompted one-shot generation.

E4.justification: v2 adds reference-framework sensitivity and agent-harness ablations, substantially redesigns the generator-bias analysis, and categorizes 164 missed vulnerabilities by CWE and pipeline stage. The Login specification failure case and per-scenario correlation analysis already existed in v1 Appendix B and are relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 adds Spearman rank correlations and linear-regression calibration fitted to neutral models. The three-sample versus single-sample policy and expert inter-rater agreement reporting remain. No increased repetition count or new confidence-interval reporting is established.

E6.justification: Model scores, per-CWE results, and confusion matrices change, with the functional comparison pool increasing from 3,109 to 5,438 solutions. These are not matched-pool performance gains. New results include rank correlations of 0.93 and 0.91 and harness comparisons. The expert-rating table is unchanged. v2 reports 80.9% functional agreement, although Figure 5 implies approximately 81.1%.

T1.justification: The mathematical and algorithmic content is substantively unchanged. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs; the new correlation and regression analyses are empirical statistical procedures.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain unchanged. v2 removes the introduction's claim that the best model achieves below 9% accuracy on hard tasks, inconsistent with the retained 25% sec_pass@1 result. Its conclusion strengthens the claim of sustained evaluation to inherently contamination-free evaluation.

C2.justification: v1 discusses mild generation bias; v2 interprets its redesigned controlled comparison as evidence against systematic self-bias. It adds explanations of framework effects and missed vulnerabilities, and explicitly discusses audit scope and unexplored difficulty limits. Appendix A.7 also introduces an incorrect interpretation: missed vulnerabilities would inflate, rather than underestimate, sec_pass@1.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents Python-FastAPI reference generation, model sampling categories, the GPT-4o tokenizer, disabled web search, and additional output-validation details. It supplies harness prompts and the audit questionnaire, and identifies reviewers as three co-authors and one coworker. These are disclosures, not evidence that the retained study changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of DualGauge, CVE-Bench, and newer offensive-agent work. It removes the broad characterization of repository-derived security tests as restricted to memory vulnerabilities and sharpens its distinction from benchmarks relying on disclosed CVEs. The principal positioning relative to BaxBench remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. The evaluation narrative is reorganized, Discussion becomes Limitations and Outlook, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. Appendix material is reorganized while the detailed prompts remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: The main paper adopts a two-column layout, updates the overview example, adds a benchmark-instance diagram, and combines the confusion matrices. The small ablation bar chart is replaced by calibrated scatterplots. New framework/harness tables, a false-negative chart, and an audit form substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The controlled 40-scenario ablation replaces v1's very small, potentially confounded bias study, substantially strengthening validation of the benchmark's evaluation signal. Framework and harness checks, failure analysis, and clearer audit disclosures further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the remaining overclaims and introduced errors, particularly the reversed interpretation of missed vulnerabilities in Appendix A.7; the evidence still does not establish inherently contamination-free evaluation.
